![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/84cfc63faa3514c7b6151d5ab8f3f8e4e7deaafa8739fa637af2f0ce7453b7fb.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,1)$ and $B(5,4).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy)=2x-2x=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,1)$ to $B(5,4)$ and  ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/18b1a5bdc11ca3c2b4b728cf8df3a3e1c4b6c2fbbe86549e9ad773367495c533.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2xy=-2(4t+1)(3t+1)=-24{t}^{2}-14t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$
